rationale: Isaac’s blessing on Jacob says, "may the sons of your mother bow down to you" (27:29, BSB). Twenty years later Jacob "bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother" (33:3), and his household "bowed down" (33:6-7). The English link is loose ("bow down" against "bowed"), but the Hebrew on Sefaria has the same verb (hishtachavah, Strong’s 7812 in Bible Hub’s interlinear for 27:29 and 33:3) twice in 27:29 and four times in Genesis 33: at 33:3, 33:6 and twice in 33:7 (script count). The blessing’s "master of your brothers" (gevir, Strong’s 1376) is a different word from the "my lord" (adoni) Jacob uses to Esau. A named reader draws the contrast: Calvin, on 27:40, says Jacob "was so far from having obtained dominion over his brother, that on his return from Padan-aram, he suppliantly tendered him his obedience," and on 33:3 he states the objection that Jacob thereby "depreciated his right of primogeniture" and answers it (see the lesson’s Positions 3). Graded contrast_reversal, following conn-gen18-righteous-few-ezekiel14, because the later scene inverts the earlier wording with the same verb. Graded plausible, not strong, because Genesis 33 does not refer back to the blessing, the verb is a common one for bowing (Abraham to the Hittites, 23:7; Joseph’s brothers, 42:6), and readers differ on whether the bowing undoes, defers or has nothing to do with the blessing. The row records the inversion and does not decide that question.
